findings.evidence: Broker Budget starts before Docker create/start; ContainerSession starts deadline later. Provider snapshots remaining seconds before staging then grants that full duration again at subprocess start. Submission path lacks explicit post-read/post-collection budget check.
findings.fix: Create one controller-owned absolute deadline at chosen published start boundary, pass it to session/watchdog/model transport/tool calls; recompute remaining at actual launch; define submission receipt cutoff separately from bounded host verification/cleanup. Reject or mark late submissions; do not reset deadline during staging/resume.
findings.impact: Undercharges or overcharges task windows and can accept work during a container grace window after the published broker cutoff; different startup/transport overhead changes available work.
findings.tests: Inject delayed container start/provider staging; assert exact same expires_at and no new model/CPU work after cutoff, including submission found near deadline.
findings.title: One numeric wall allowance creates multiple inconsistent absolute deadlines

findings.evidence: cpu.run invokes python /work/science.py without reading/hashing/snapshotting its entry point; final artifact hashes reflect later state. A normal agent can revise scripts after runs, and an adversarial background worker can change them before execution.
findings.fix: Snapshot and hash the selected entry-point bytes in controller custody before execution, execute those frozen bytes rather than rereading mutable path; record argv/cwd/container ID/start/end/output receipt with the same execution ID. Record dependency/input snapshot boundaries and distinguish unobserved direct worker compute. Recompute selected scientific quantities from submitted code when needed.
findings.impact: Judge cannot connect a reported experiment to the exact historical implementation, even with genuine command return codes. Solver-authored result files/RPC text must not substitute for this missing platform evidence.
findings.tests: Mutate a script after submission and concurrently before exec; platform execution must remain tied to frozen entry hash, and old/new versions remain separately inspectable.
findings.title: CPU execution is recorded by mutable path, not bound to executed code bytes

findings.evidence: Assets are checked before ContainerSession copies them, but input_hashes is omitted. task.json is independently read/hashed/copied, so broker view and worker view can differ after a concurrent modification. Harness invocation hash is also separate from final release snapshot.
findings.fix: Freeze public task/harness/worker/assets once; pass expected hashes for every published file to ContainerSession. Construct broker view and invocation hashes from that same frozen snapshot. Validate public TaskView and use contained() before path resolution to reject links/aliases, rather than relying on resolve().is_symlink().
findings.impact: Frozen-version and fixed-input guarantees are not enforced at publication; a valid source edit between phases can silently run another version. This is an integrity risk, not a demonstrated private-data exfiltration.
findings.tests: Mutate each source after precheck but before copy; fail closed. Worker task hash must equal broker view snapshot/hash and invocation manifest.
findings.title: Verified release hashes are not enforced when creating actual container inputs

findings.fix: Separate controller-private RPC audit from collected solver artifacts. Exclude reserved .broker and .process trees, or explicitly segregate/tag all such copies as untrusted diagnostics; collect declared artifacts under independent byte/entry quotas and preserve host-sourced execution receipts separately. Judge must only treat actual broker/session audit as platform evidence.
findings.impact: The same-UID harness can forge .broker requests/responses/submission and .process statuses. Actual host broker RPC records are trustworthy for dispatch, but exported copies are not. Unqualified downstream inclusion risks promoting fabricated traces; internal transport bytes also consume scientific artifact quotas and can reject otherwise small valid submissions.
findings.tests: Forge a .broker response claiming a CPU/model call never made; verify no trusted execution receipt is produced and judge publication cannot label that file platform trace. Internal messages must not exhaust the declared scientific-artifact quota.
findings.title: Solver-writable control-lookalike files are exported among scientific artifacts

findings.evidence: Requests/submissions may be read up to 2,000,000 bytes, but response is passed to session.write whose bound defaults to 1MiB. A bounded cpu.run may return ~1MiB stdout plus JSON envelope and stderr, exceeding that bound.
findings.fix: Use a common explicitly published RPC response limit and bounded serialization; truncate stdout/stderr to leave JSON overhead, or provide controller-stored result handles with bounded chunked reads. Do not silently truncate scientific data.
findings.impact: A legal broker tool result can fail response publication, aborting an otherwise valid run as an infrastructure issue.
findings.tests: Return stdout near cap with non-ASCII/JSON-escaped bytes and both streams; transport must either deliver complete legal response or return a typed recoverable capacity error.
findings.title: Response envelope bound exceeds write transport capacity

findings.evidence: Generated harness runs unrestricted Python inside the bounded task container and can read /inputs, write /work, spawn CPU subprocesses or compute directly without calling ToolClient.
findings.fix: Document tool_calls as broker API request accounting, rely on container resource budgets for arbitrary harness compute, and do not equate absent cpu.run trace with no computation. If a task truly requires restricting a tool privilege, enforce that capability outside the worker rather than only in Python API.
findings.impact: Container CPU/RAM/PID/time limits remain enforced, and model calls remain broker-controlled; however absent cpu_python_execution or exhausted tool_calls do not forbid all CPU/file activity. Claims that they do would be false.
findings.tests: Harness performs direct calculation with zero broker tool calls; expected classification and metric semantics must be explicit.
findings.title: Tool counter measures broker requests, not arbitrary Python computation/file operations

positive_controls: Provider/role/deadline arguments not accepted from worker RPC
Model attempts charged before provider invocation; replayed sequence rejected
Host errors redacted from worker response
Readonly /inputs and no credentials/socket/network preserved by ContainerSession
Artifact hash rechecked against captured bytes after collection
Run status explicitly structural development, not scientific success; worker status already marked untrusted
scope: Read-only independent review of executor broker/worker integration; no model calls and no root code edits
timeout_artifact_options: Current honest option: export declared checkpoints while alive; if timeout occurs, record remaining artifact loss as platform limitation, not scientific absence.
Stronger design: one fresh dedicated Docker volume backed by filesystem with actual per-volume byte/inode quota, not a host writable bind; verify ENOSPC, owner-only cleanup, no cross-task reuse.

Alternative: bounded controller checkpoint broker snapshots on successful tool return / explicit submit, subject to controller storage caps; retain immutable host snapshots before session kill. This preserves last checkpoint, not arbitrary last-millisecond state.
verdict: Revise before claiming accepted formal execution or using trace as exact scientific provenance
